Welcome back to Git and GitHub Deep Mastery.

Five topics. Static analysis: what scanners find in workflow files, and what they can't know.

slides.headline: The review checklist
slides.body: Use it on every pull request that touches .github/workflows/, an action definition, or a script that a workflow runs.

slides.direction: The checklist of section 21A.19, one item at a time.
items: Trigger. Does the change add or keep pull_request_target, workflow_run, issue_comment, issues or discussion? If so, which outsider-controlled input reaches the job?
Checkout. Any ref: or repository: taken from the event? Any allow-unsafe-pr-checkout? Any git fetch or gh pr checkout of pull request code in a privileged job?
Permissions. Is there a top-level permissions block, read-only? Is each write scope on the one job that needs it? Did the change widen anything?
Expressions. Is there any ${{ }} inside run:, or inside an input that is evaluated as code? Including multi-line scripts?
Actions. Is every uses: a 40-character commit ID from the action's own repository, with a version comment? Is a new action necessary, and who maintains it?

Privileged jobs. For each job that publishes, deploys or holds id-token: write: does it run only on trusted refs, behind an environment, with cache-mode: none or read, and with no artifact from an untrusted run executed?

slides.body: A picture helps. Hold workflow 12 as a reference shape, and review other workflows as differences from it.
The shape has two zones. An open zone, where outsiders' code and text are allowed in: the test job, the title job, the dependency review.
Every item of the checklist asks one of two things.
Where the model needs a warning, and the textbook gives it in section 21A.21: the edge case behind most incidents is two safe-looking workflows that share something.
Try it now, thirty seconds, on paper.

slides.direction: Workflow 12 as an outline. Draw the file's skeleton first, then add one bracket at a time on the right, each labelled with the attack class it answers.
slides.text:
on: pull_request, push to main                      ]  fork code never runs next to secrets
  permissions: contents: read                         ]  a compromised step with a write token
  concurrency: ...                                    ]  overlapping runs

  jobs:
    test:                         timeout-minutes     ]  runaway runs
      uses: checkout@<commit ID>                      ]  a moved tag
        persist-credentials: false                    ]  later steps using the token through Git
      uses: setup-uv@<commit ID>
      run: uv sync --locked / ruff / pytest

    pr-metadata:   permissions: {}                    ]  a job that needs no access gets none
      env: PR_TITLE: ${{ ...title }}                  ]  script injection
      run: (a constant script that reads "$PR_TITLE")

    dependency-review:  permissions: contents: read

    deploy-staging:
      if: push && refs/heads/main && ...              ]  unreviewed code reaching the identity
      environment: staging                            ]  a deployment without rules; fixes the OIDC subject
      permissions: contents: read, id-token: write    ]  any other job requesting a cloud token
      cache-mode: none                                ]  a poisoned cache next to the identity
      uses: configure-aws-credentials@<commit ID>     ]  no stored cloud key

slides.headline: One more thing a reviewer must get right: the base
slides.body: Find where a comment is attached to a single line of the diff, and where the overall verdict is chosen: approve, comment, or request changes.
Five mistakes to watch for.

items: Treating a green scanner as a review. Root cause: a scanner finds patterns; it does not know which job holds the credential that matters, and it does not find lines that are missing.
Reviewing only the changed lines. Root cause: an unchanged step means something else after the trigger above it changed; read the new file whole.
Reviewing one workflow at a time. Root cause: most incidents involve two safe-looking workflows that share a cache, an artifact, a label or a branch.

Giving an agent's job the permissions the team would have. Root cause: the agent reads attacker-controlled text, and for an agent text is instruction; through the prompt the pull request author partly wrote the job.
Reading a two-dot diff of the pull request. Root cause: two dots compare the tips, so changes made on the base branch appear as if the author had made them.

slides.body: Now, out of the lab. A team adds an LLM reviewer to its repository of evaluation code.
Run the checklist. Item one: a privileged trigger, and the outsider-controlled input is the entire content of the pull request, handed to the agent as text.
The textbook's recommendation applies point by point.
The team's rule afterwards is the chapter's sentence, pinned in the repository: give the agent's job permissions as if the pull request author had written the job.
Your turn. Do Lab 29.3, "Review a pull request that changes workflows", in lab-manual/m29-actions-security.md, in labs/shell.
Write review.md: one comment per finding, each with the file and line, a severity, what the line does, what an attacker could achieve, and the requested change.
The challenge is Exercise 29.7, "Benchmark scores on fork pull requests", in exercises/m26-m31-actions-security.md.

items: A scanner finds patterns in workflow files; it does not know which job holds the credential that matters, so you run one and still read the file.
From 2025 to 2026 the platform moved its defaults toward these controls, with 2 November 2026 as the next announced date; each change has something it does not cover.
Workflow 12 keeps outsiders' code and text in jobs without privilege, and keeps its one identity in a job that only trusted code can reach, behind an environment, without a cache.
An agent in a workflow reads attacker-controlled text and holds credentials; give its job permissions as if the pull request author had written it.
The checklist has eleven items: trigger, checkout, permissions, expressions, actions, remote code, secrets, privileged jobs, runner, credentials in Git, process.

slides.body: Read sections 21A.14 to 21A.17 and 21A.19 to 21A.22 of Chapter 21A.
Today you audited a workflow with five questions and read a risky diff with eleven.

beats.text: "Contributors from forks could not see coverage on their pull requests because the token is missing there. This switches CI to the trigger that has secrets, adds the coverage uploader and a comment, moves CI to our own runner to save minutes, and adds a release workflow that publishes to PyPI on a version tag."

beats.text: Three words first. A workflow is a file that tells GitHub Actions which jobs to run when an event happens. A pull request proposes merging a branch, and a reviewer reads its diff, the lines it adds and removes. And static analysis means reading a file for risky patterns without running it.

beats.text: Five topics. Static analysis: what scanners find in workflow files, and what they can't know. The platform changes of 2025 and 2026, as one dated list. And the review checklist of section 21A.19: eleven items for every pull request that touches a workflow.

beats.text: CodeQL for workflows is part of GitHub code scanning, the analysis of code for vulnerabilities and coding errors. It has been generally available since the twenty-second of April 2025, and default setup enables it when workflow files exist on the default branch. It finds, in the changelog's words, "missing required permissions, dangerous inputs without proper validation, and script injection vulnerabilities", and since CodeQL 2.26.4 also mutable references to reusable workflows.

beats.text: The twenty-second of April 2025: CodeQL analysis of workflow files generally available. The fifteenth of August 2025: the allowed-actions policy can block entries and require full commit pins. The twenty-eighth of October 2025: immutable releases, whose tag can no longer be moved, generally available. The eighth of December 2025: pull_request_target always uses the workflow from the default branch, and environment branch rules follow the execution ref.

The eighth of December 2025: `pull_request_target` always uses the workflow from the default branch, and environment branch rules follow the execution ref.

beats.text: The fifth of February 2026: action allow-listing on all plans. The twenty-third of April and the fifteenth of July 2026: immutable OIDC subject claims, opt-in and then default for new repositories. The eighteenth of June and the twentieth of July 2026: the checkout action at version 7 refuses fork pull request code under privileged triggers, then back-ported. The twenty-sixth of June 2026: a read-only default-branch cache for low-trust triggers. The fourteenth of July 2026: a default cooldown, a waiting period, for Dependabot version updates.

beats.text: The twenty-eighth of July 2026: runs "identified as potentially malicious" are held until a collaborator with write access approves them, in public repositories only, with no configuration. The tenth of September 2026: cache-mode. The seventeenth of September 2026: workflow execution protections generally available. And the second of November 2026: the date GitHub announced for enforcing the default rule that disables pull_request_target in affected public repositories. Check the changelog on the day you watch this.

beats.text: Workflow 12. The file puts the controls in one place: a test job, a job that reads the pull request title, a dependency review, and a staging deployment through OIDC, the exchange that replaces a stored cloud key. It was assembled from documented syntax and input names and parse-checked. It was not executed on GitHub by the author. Lab 29.2 has you run it.
beats.tele: Workflow 12. The file puts the controls in one place: a test job, a job that reads the pull request title, a dependency review, and a staging deployment through OIDC, the exchange that replaces a stored cloud key. It was assembled from documented syntax and input names and parse-checked. It was not executed on GitHub by the author. Lab 29.2 has you run it.

beats.text: The textbook reads it with five questions, which grep can answer for any workflow. Which events start it? What may the token do? Whose code runs, and is every reference a full commit ID? Where does an expression appear, and is any of them inside a script? Which stored secrets does it read? You'll run all five in a moment.

beats.text: Then the controls, each with the threat it answers.
beats.tele: Then the controls, each with the threat it answers.

beats.text: permissions: contents: read at the top, an empty map for the title job, and per-job additions below: against a compromised step using a write token.
beats.tele: `permissions: contents: read` at the top, an empty map for the title job, and per-job additions below: against a compromised step using a write token.

beats.text: on: pull_request: against fork code running next to secrets.
beats.tele: `on: pull_request`: against fork code running next to secrets.

beats.text: Every uses is a commit ID with a version comment: against a moved tag.
beats.tele: Every `uses` is a commit ID with a version comment: against a moved tag.

beats.text: persist-credentials: false on every checkout: against later steps using the token through Git.
beats.tele: `persist-credentials: false` on every checkout: against later steps using the token through Git.

beats.text: The title only under env: against script injection.
beats.tele: The title only under `env`: against script injection.

beats.text: The deployment if requires a push to main: against unreviewed code reaching the cloud identity.
beats.tele: The deployment `if` requires a push to `main`: against unreviewed code reaching the cloud identity.

beats.text: environment: staging: against a deployment without the environment's rules. It also fixes the OIDC subject.
beats.tele: `environment: staging`: against a deployment without the environment's rules. It also fixes the OIDC subject.

beats.text: id-token: write on one job only: against any other job requesting a cloud token.
beats.tele: `id-token: write` on one job only: against any other job requesting a cloud token.

beats.text: cache-mode: none on the deployment job: against a poisoned cache executing next to the cloud identity.
beats.tele: `cache-mode: none` on the deployment job: against a poisoned cache executing next to the cloud identity.

beats.text: timeout-minutes and concurrency: against runaway or overlapping runs.
beats.tele: `timeout-minutes` and `concurrency`: against runaway or overlapping runs.

beats.text: And what the file doesn't do, which the textbook lists as carefully as what it does. It doesn't attest the build. It doesn't scan itself. Add CodeQL default setup for that. And the staging role's trust policy lives in the cloud account, where the workflow can't enforce it.

beats.text: AI agents inside workflows. An agent in a workflow, whether an LLM reviewer, a triage bot or a coding agent, combines parts three and four of the model in a new form. An LLM is a large language model, a program that reads text and writes text. The agent reads attacker-controlled text and holds credentials. And for an agent, text is instruction. The textbook's sentence: no env trick separates data from code in a prompt.
beats.tele: AI agents inside workflows. An agent in a workflow, whether an LLM reviewer, a triage bot or a coding agent, combines parts three and four of the model in a new form. The textbook's sentence: no `env` trick separates data from code in a prompt.

beats.text: Two findings from the report, with their flags. An automated account ran a week-long campaign in February and March 2026 that combined pull_request_target abuse, branch-name and filename injection, and prompt injection, instructions hidden in the text an agent reads, against an AI reviewer.
beats.tele: Two findings from the report, with their flags. An automated account ran a week-long campaign in February and March 2026 that combined `pull_request_target` abuse, branch-name and filename injection, and prompt injection, instructions hidden in the text an agent reads, against an AI reviewer.

beats.text: And researchers reported in April 2026 that AI coding agents run as GitHub Actions could be steered by text in pull request titles, issue bodies or comments into revealing CI secrets. The textbook marks the second: this is secondary reporting only, and the primary write-up was not fetched.
beats.tele: And researchers reported in April 2026 that AI coding agents run as GitHub Actions could be steered by text in pull request titles, issue bodies or comments into revealing CI secrets. The textbook marks the second: this is secondary reporting only, and the primary write-up was not fetched.

beats.text: The report's recommendation, which it labels as an inference. An agent in a workflow gets a dedicated low-privilege, spend-capped key. No write token unless required. And it doesn't run automatically on untrusted contributions. Then the chapter's own formulation, which is the one to remember: give the agent's job permissions as if the pull request author had written the job, because through the prompt they partly did.
beats.tele: The report's recommendation, which it labels as an inference. An agent in a workflow gets a dedicated low-privilege, spend-capped key. No write token unless required. And it doesn't run automatically on untrusted contributions. Then the chapter's own formulation, which is the one to remember: give the agent's job `permissions` as if the pull request author had written the job, because through the prompt they partly did.

beats.text: The review checklist. Use it on every pull request that touches .github/workflows/, an action definition, or a script that a workflow runs. Eleven items.
beats.tele: The review checklist. Use it on every pull request that touches `.github/workflows/`, an action definition, or a script that a workflow runs. Eleven items.

beats.text: One, trigger. Does the change add or keep pull_request_target, workflow_run, issue_comment, issues or discussion? If so, which outsider-controlled input reaches the job?
beats.tele: One, trigger. Does the change add or keep `pull_request_target`, `workflow_run`, `issue_comment`, `issues` or `discussion`? If so, which outsider-controlled input reaches the job?

beats.text: Two, checkout. Any ref or repository taken from the event? Any allow-unsafe-pr-checkout? Any git fetch or gh pr checkout of pull request code in a privileged job?
beats.tele: Two, checkout. Any `ref` or `repository` taken from the event? Any `allow-unsafe-pr-checkout`? Any `git fetch` or `gh pr checkout` of pull request code in a privileged job?

beats.text: Three, permissions. Is there a top-level permissions block, read-only? Is each write scope on the one job that needs it? Did the change widen anything?
beats.tele: Three, permissions. Is there a top-level `permissions` block, read-only? Is each write scope on the one job that needs it? Did the change widen anything?

beats.text: Four, expressions. Is there any expression inside run, or inside an input that is evaluated as code? Including multi-line scripts?
beats.tele: Four, expressions. Is there any expression inside `run`, or inside an input that is evaluated as code? Including multi-line scripts?

beats.text: Five, actions. Is every uses a 40-character commit ID from the action's own repository, with a version comment? Is a new action necessary, and who maintains it?
beats.tele: Five, actions. Is every `uses` a 40-character commit ID from the action's own repository, with a version comment? Is a new action necessary, and who maintains it?

beats.text: Six, remote code. Any download piped into a shell, or an installer fetched without a checksum?
beats.tele: Six, remote code. Any download piped into a shell, or an installer fetched without a checksum?

beats.text: Seven, secrets. Is each secret referenced in the narrowest place: one step, in a job behind an environment? Could OIDC replace it? Does any secret appear on a command line?
beats.tele: Seven, secrets. Is each secret referenced in the narrowest place: one step, in a job behind an environment? Could OIDC replace it? Does any secret appear on a command line?

beats.text: Eight, privileged jobs. For each job that publishes, deploys or holds id-token: write: does it run only on trusted refs, behind an environment, with cache-mode set to none or read, and with no artifact from an untrusted run executed?
beats.tele: Eight, privileged jobs. For each job that publishes, deploys or holds `id-token: write`: does it run only on trusted refs, behind an environment, with `cache-mode` set to `none` or `read`, and with no artifact from an untrusted run executed?

beats.text: Nine, runner. Did runs-on change to a self-hosted label? For which events?
beats.tele: Nine, runner. Did `runs-on` change to a self-hosted label? For which events?

beats.text: Ten, credentials in Git. persist-credentials: false wherever the job doesn't push?
beats.tele: Ten, credentials in Git. `persist-credentials: false` wherever the job doesn't push?

beats.text: Eleven, process. Was the change reviewed by a code owner of the workflows directory, and does a ruleset require that? Does a workflow scanner run on the pull request?
beats.tele: Eleven, process. Was the change reviewed by a code owner of the workflows directory, and does a ruleset require that? Does a workflow scanner run on the pull request?

beats.text: A picture helps. Hold workflow 12 as a reference shape, and review other workflows as differences from it.
beats.tele: A picture helps. Hold workflow 12 as a reference shape, and review other workflows as differences from it.

beats.text: The shape has two zones. An open zone, where outsiders' code and text are allowed in: the test job, the title job, the dependency review. In that zone the token is read-only or absent, there are no secrets, and untrusted text is only ever data. And a closed zone, the deployment job, where an identity lives. Nothing from outside gets in: only a push to main, behind an environment, with no cache.
beats.tele: The shape has two zones. An open zone, where outsiders' code and text are allowed in: the test job, the title job, the dependency review. In that zone the token is read-only or absent, there are no secrets, and untrusted text is only ever data. And a closed zone, the deployment job, where an identity lives. Nothing from outside gets in: only a push to `main`, behind an environment, with no cache.

beats.text: Every item of the checklist asks one of two things. Did this change let something from outside into the closed zone? Or did it move something valuable into the open zone?
beats.tele: Every item of the checklist asks one of two things. Did this change let something from outside into the closed zone? Or did it move something valuable into the open zone?

beats.text: Where the model needs a warning, and the textbook gives it in section 21A.21: the edge case behind most incidents is two safe-looking workflows that share something. A low-privilege workflow that can write a cache, an artifact, a label or a branch, and a high-privilege workflow that trusts it. So the zones aren't per file. Review workflows as a set.

beats.text: Five mistakes to watch for.
beats.tele: Five mistakes to watch for.

beats.text: Treating a green scanner as a review. Root cause: a scanner finds patterns; it does not know which job holds the credential that matters, and it does not find lines that are missing.

beats.text: Reviewing only the changed lines. Root cause: an unchanged step means something else after the trigger above it changed; read the new file whole.
beats.tele: Reviewing only the changed lines. Root cause: an unchanged step means something else after the trigger above it changed; read the new file whole.

beats.text: Reviewing one workflow at a time. Root cause: most incidents involve two safe-looking workflows that share a cache, an artifact, a label or a branch.

beats.text: The textbook's recommendation applies point by point. A dedicated low-privilege, spend-capped key, so that a leak is bounded. No write token unless required: for example, the agent writes its review to the job summary, and a separate job without the model key posts it. And it doesn't run automatically on untrusted contributions: a maintainer starts it for a fork's pull request after reading the change.
